nameStory: The name 'cinquefoil' comes from the French 'cinq feuilles,' meaning 'five leaves,' referring to the plant's distinctive five-leaflet pattern. The 'shrubby' part distinguishes it from its herbaceous cousins that hug the ground. This tough little bush earned the nickname 'golden hardhack' for its brilliant yellow blooms and incredibly hardy nature.
description: Shrubby cinquefoil is a compact, rounded deciduous shrub that typically grows 2-4 feet tall and wide. It's covered in small, bright yellow flowers that look like tiny wild roses, which makes sense since it's in the rose family. The plant has a dense, twiggy appearance with small compound leaves that give it a delicate, almost ferny texture. This extremely hardy shrub can survive harsh mountain conditions and bitter cold winters.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow flowers with five rounded petals, about the size of a nickel, blooming continuously from late spring through fall. The flowers have a silky texture and numerous yellow stamens in the center, giving them a cheerful, rose-like appearance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small compound leaves with 3-7 narrow leaflets (usually 5) that feel slightly fuzzy and have smooth edges. The leaflets are arranged like fingers on a hand, and the whole leaf is only about an inch long.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Dense, mounded shrub with numerous thin, brown twigs that create a neat, rounded shape. The bark on older stems peels in thin, papery strips and feels rough to the touch.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny, dry, brown seed clusters that replace the flowers in late summer and fall, often persisting through winter and giving branches a fuzzy appearance.

habitat: Look for shrubby cinquefoil in rocky, well-drained soils in full sun, especially in mountainous areas and exposed sites. In New England, it's often found in alpine and subalpine zones, rocky slopes, and disturbed areas where other plants struggle. It's also commonly planted in landscapes and may escape cultivation, thriving in poor soils where more finicky plants fail.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green in late spring, followed quickly by the first flush of golden flowers. The contrast between fresh foliage and bright blooms makes identification easy.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with abundant yellow flowers covering the shrub continuously. This is the best time for identification as flowers and full foliage are both present.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue blooming until hard frost while leaves turn yellowish. Seed heads become more prominent as some flowers fade.
seasonality.winter: Bare brown twigs with peeling bark and persistent fuzzy seed clusters. The dense, twiggy branching pattern and rounded shape remain distinctive.

funFact: Despite being called 'cinquefoil' (five leaves), this plant doesn't actually have five leaves at all—it has compound leaves with five leaflets each, and sometimes even three or seven leaflets, making its name beautifully misleading!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with potentilla species, which makes sense since it was formerly classified as Potentilla fruticosa and still appears under that name in many garden centers. Unlike herbaceous potentillas that die back in winter, shrubby cinquefoil keeps its woody stems year-round—if it's a permanent shrub with yellow five-petaled flowers, you've got shrubby cinquefoil.
contextualKnowledge: You'll often see this plant sold in nurseries as 'Potentilla fruticosa' since that was its scientific name for over a century. Many gardeners and even some field guides still use the old name, so don't be confused if you see both names referring to the same plant. It's also known as 'kuril tea' because people in Siberia traditionally brewed the leaves into tea.
compareHints: Since shrubby cinquefoil is the only Dasiphora species in New England, compare it to other rose family shrubs with yellow flowers. Unlike wild roses which have thorns and larger flowers, shrubby cinquefoil is thornless with smaller, more numerous blooms. Unlike spicebush or witch hazel with their four-petaled yellow flowers, shrubby cinquefoil consistently has five petals and compound leaves.
